prompt: An airline cut fares 10% on one route, where most passengers are business travelers. Passengers rose 6%, and revenue on the route fell. Which is the strongest initial hypothesis?

options.text: Business travelers likely fly whatever the fare, so the cut just gave revenue away.
options.feedback: Right. Most passengers travel for work and their employers pay, so a lower fare barely changes how many fly: 0.9 × 1.06 ≈ 0.95, a revenue fall of about 5%. I'd compare passenger growth by traveler type.

options.text: Leisure travelers have probably flooded the route, crowding out business fares.
options.feedback: Passengers rose only 6%, so there was no flood.

options.text: The cut was probably small enough that travelers didn't notice.
options.feedback: Passengers did rise 6%, so it was noticed. The issue is that 6% more passengers can't make up a 10% lower fare.

options.text: The fare cut probably didn't land the way it was meant to.
options.feedback: Too vague to test: it doesn't say why or what data would show it.

explanation: The data shows a 10% fare cut with 6% more passengers, a revenue loss of about 5% (0.9 × 1.06). Likely cause: business travelers, whose employers pay, barely respond to price. To test it, compare passenger growth by traveler type. If leisure travelers also barely responded, demand on the route is simply insensitive to price.
